title: Education, Not Entertainment
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart contends that schools cannot and should not try to out-entertain a world of customized, on-demand media. Even if they could, he argues, the result would be something much lower than an education. He urges teachers not to feel bad that students do not find them entertaining but to keep modeling something more compelling and timeless. Using examples like Things Fall Apart, the Sepoy Mutiny and an article about Saudi Arabia, he shows that initially boring content becomes engaging once students are taught to enter it. He closes by comparing education to the mundane tasks of marriage and parenting, whose value emerges only through effort, and concludes that engagement is not entertainment.
points: Competing with YouTube-era entertainment is a losing and mistaken goal for schools.
Teachers should model something more lasting than entertainment instead of apologizing for being less entertaining.
Initially boring texts become compelling when students are taught the moves for entering them.
Hard content should not be avoided just because it is boring at first.
Engagement and entertainment are distinct, as the unglamorous work of family life shows.
quotes: We are currently teaching the most entertained generation in the history of humankind. I don't say that disparagingly; my generation is not morally superior to the students I teach simply because we had access to exponentially less entertainment.

Here is my point: it is madness for our schools to try to out-entertain the world. It is madness because we can't; much more so, it's madness because even if we could, we'd be achieving something much lower than an education.
Don't feel bad that your students don't find you entertaining. Feel bad if you are not in front of them attempting to model something more compelling and timeless than entertainment.

What I am saying is that we ought not to avoid teaching our kids to read Things Fall Apart or five primary sources about the Sepoy Mutiny or how to divide fractions just because some students may find these things initially boring.
But something happens when we actually take our students seriously enough to teach them to read and discuss texts like these.

There's just nothing sexy about changing a diaper, disciplining a child, learning to fold laundry “correctly” or having meetings about the family budget — at least not to me. I'd be far more entertained watching YouTube.
Education, I think, should be kind of the same way. Engagement is much different than entertainment.
